html:
Indigo, a blue dye from a tropical plant, was the chief export of colonial El Salvador from the late 1500s until the mid-1800s. The province was the main indigo producer of Central America.

The plant, called xiquilite, was grown on estates and soaked and beaten in vats to make dye cakes, which went to Guatemala City and then to Europe for its textile mills. The work was hard and unhealthy, and the Spanish crown tried, often in vain, to keep Indigenous people out of the vats. Merchants in Guatemala controlled the trade, which bred resentment in San Salvador.

When synthetic dyes from Germany took over the market in the late 1800s, Salvadoran landowners turned to coffee. The indigo trade shaped the Pipil lands and the estates of El Salvador, as logwood did in Belize.
